summary: Routing systems have been controlled by relatively static policies, but data centers, on-demand WAN services and dynamic policies need more dynamic programming. This informational RFC states the problem the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers are usually set up by hand and change their own routes on their own. Software that wants to steer traffic across a data centre has no standard way to ask a router to do it, or to read back what the router thinks its network looks like. This document describes the problem and the shape of a proposed interface.

why not use snmp to configure routers
what is the interface to the routing system
subtitle: Why routers need a fast, programmable, standard interface that software can use to read and change routing state.

tldr.problem: Routers are still programmed by relatively static policies, but data centres, on-demand WAN services and dynamic traffic steering need routing to be changed on the fly and by software.
tldr.mechanism: The document proposes an Interface to the Routing System, in which a client talks to an agent inside the router over a protocol with data models for the routing information base, the policy database, topology and measurements.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement rather than a specification: it lists what a protocol would have to do and explains why the three existing management interfaces are not the answer.

facts.label: Latency target
facts.value: Simple operations complete within a sub-second timescale

today: RFC 7920 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the problem statement for the Interface to the Routing System work. It describes no protocol of its own; the architecture it points at is in RFC 7921, and the data models and protocols it calls for were to be defined separately.

sections.title: Why a New Interface Is Needed
sections.content:
Traditionally, routing systems have implemented routing and signalling, for example MPLS, to control traffic forwarding. Route computation has been controlled by relatively static policies that define link cost, route cost, or import and export routing policies. The advent of highly dynamic data-centre networking, on-demand WAN services, dynamic policy-driven traffic steering and service chaining, the need for real-time security threat responsiveness through traffic control, and a paradigm of separating policy-based decision-making from the router itself have created the need to manage and program routing systems more dynamically, in order to control routing information and traffic paths and to extract network topology information, traffic statistics and other network analytics from routing systems.

As networks grow in scale and complexity and desired policy becomes more complex and dynamic, there is a need to support rapid control and analytics. The scale of modern networks and data centres and the associated operational expense drives the need to automate even the simplest operations, and the ability to interact quickly through more complex operations is even more critical. For network applications to have access to and control over information in different vendors' routing systems, a publicly documented interface is required. It needs to support real-time, asynchronous interactions using efficient data models and encodings based on and extending those previously defined, and it must be tailored to provide a solid base on which a variety of use cases can be supported.

To support orchestration software and automated network applications that dynamically modify the network, there is a need to learn topology, network analytics and existing state from the network, as well as to create or modify routing information and network paths. A feedback loop is needed so that changes can be verifiable and the applications can learn and react to network changes. Proprietary solutions that partially support these requirements have been developed for specific situations, and standardizing an interface is expected to make it easier to integrate into a network; because those partial solutions already exist, the document argues that standardizing a common interface should be feasible.

Appendix A explains why the three existing management interfaces are not the answer. The command-line interface is the most popular way to configure a device and learn its state. It is proprietary, resembles a UNIX shell, allows very customised control and observation, and exists in some form on almost every device. Processing what it returns, called screen scraping, is burdensome because the data is formatted for a human operator and the layout can vary from device to device and between software versions. Despite its ubiquity it has never been standardised, is unlikely ever to be, and is not a candidate solution.

SNMP with its MIB modules is the second most popular way to interrogate a device's state, statistics and configuration, and has a long history of being used by network managers to gather information about routing systems. It is very rarely used to configure a device, for reasons that vary by operator, including complexity, the lack of desired configuration semantics such as rollback, sandboxing or versioning, and the difficulty of using the semantics defined in the MIB modules. It too is not a candidate. NETCONF, the IETF's Network Configuration Protocol, has made many strides past those configuration limitations, but as a new technology with an initial lack of standard data models its adoption has been slow. As needed, I2RS will identify and define the information and data models to support its applications, and extensions to handle multi-headed control may need to be added to NETCONF and its data models.
sections.plainLanguage: The document explains why the usual ways of managing a router will not do. The command line is proprietary and its output is written for people to read, SNMP is good for looking but not for changing, and NETCONF is promising but still new. A new interface is needed.

sections.title: The I2RS Model
sections.content:
Managing a network of systems running a variety of routing protocols, or providing one or more additional services such as forwarding, classification and policing or firewalling, involves interactions between multiple components within those systems. Some of these systems or components may be virtualised, co-located in the same physical system, or distributed. In all cases it is desirable to enable network applications to manage and control the services provided by many, if not all, of these components, subject to authenticated and authorised access and policies.

A data-model-driven interface to the routing system is needed. It allows expansion of what information can be read and controlled and allows for future flexibility. At least one accompanying protocol with clearly defined operations is needed; the suitable protocols can be identified and expanded to support the requirements of an Interface to the Routing System, and the solutions must be designed to facilitate rapid, isolated, secure and dynamic changes to a device's routing system, which would facilitate wide-scale deployment of interoperable applications and routing systems.

The model has an I2RS client and an I2RS agent, and the selected protocols extend between them. The I2RS agent is associated with a routing element, which may or may not be co-located with a data plane. The I2RS client could be integrated in a network application, or controlled and used by one or more separate network applications. For instance, an I2RS client could be provided by a network controller or a network orchestration system that presents a non-I2RS interface to network applications and an I2RS interface to the agents on the systems being managed. All other objects and interfaces in the model figure are outside the I2RS scope for standardisation, and the scope of the data models used by I2RS extends across the entire routing system and the selected protocols.

I2RS uses a set of meaningful data models for information in the routing system and in a topology database. Each data model should describe the meaning and relationships of the modelled items. The models should be separable across different features of the managed components, versioned and extendable. I2RS needs to interact with several logical components of the routing element: the policy database, the topology database, the subscription and configuration for dynamic measurements and events, the routing and signalling protocols, and the Routing Information Base manager. This interaction is for writing, for example to policy databases or the RIB manager, as well as for reading, for example dynamic measurement or the topology database. An application should be able to combine data from individual routing elements to provide network-wide data models.

The data models should translate into a concise transfer syntax, sent via the I2RS protocol, that is straightforward for applications to use, for example a web services design paradigm. The information transfer should use existing transport protocols to provide the reliability, security and timeliness appropriate for the particular data.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture has two halves. Software acts as a client, a piece of software inside the router acts as an agent, and a protocol runs between them. The agent sits in front of the router's internal parts: its policy database, its topology database, its routing protocols and its forwarding table.

sections.title: Data Models for Routing State
sections.content:
There is a need to be able to precisely control routing and signalling state based on policy or external measures. One set of data models I2RS should focus on is for interacting with the RIB layer, for example the RIB, the Label Information Base, the multicast RIB and policy-based routing, to provide flexibility and routing abstractions. The desired routing and signalling state might range from simple static routes to policy-based routing, to static multicast replication and routing state. To usefully model next hops, the data model employed needs to handle next-hop indirection and recursion, such as a prefix X routed like prefix Y, as well as different types of tunnelling and encapsulation.

Efforts to provide this level of control have focused on standardising data models that describe the forwarding plane, for example the Forwarding and Control Element Separation framework in RFC 3746. I2RS takes a different view: the routing system and a router's operating system provide useful mechanisms that applications could harness to accomplish application-level goals. Using routing indirection, recursion and common routing abstractions such as tunnels and Label Switched Paths provides significant flexibility over collapsing the state to individual routes in the Forwarding Information Base that need to be individually modified when a change occurs.

In addition to interfaces to control the RIB layer, there is a need to dynamically configure policies and parameter values for the various routing and signalling protocols based on application-level policy decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: The data has to describe the router's routing table, not just the forwarding table, and it has to handle a route that points at another route. That way one change can be expressed in the way an operator writes it, instead of rewriting every individual entry.

sections.title: Learning What the Router Knows
sections.content:
A router holds information that applications may require so that they can understand the network, verify that programmed state is installed, measure the behaviour of various flows, and understand the existing configuration and state of the router. I2RS should provide a framework so that applications can register for asynchronous notifications and can make specific requests for information.

Although there are efforts to extend the topological information available, even the best of these, such as BGP Link State in RFC 7752, still provide only the current active state as seen at the IGP and BGP layers. Detailed topological state that provides more information than the current functional status, such as active paths and links, is needed by applications. Examples of missing information include paths or links that are potentially available, for example administratively down, or unknown, for example to peers or customers, to the routing topology.

For applications to have a feedback loop that includes awareness of the relevant traffic, an application must be able to request the measurement and timely, scalable reporting of data. While a mechanism such as IP Flow Information Export in RFC 5470 may be the facilitator for delivering the data, providing the ability for an application to dynamically request that measurements be taken and data delivered is important.

There is also a wide range of events that applications could use to support verification of router state before other network state is changed, for example that a route has been installed, and to allow timely action in response to changes of relevant routes by others or to router events such as link up or down. While a few of these, such as link up and down, may be available through MIB notifications today, the full range is not, for example route installed, route changed or primary LSP changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Software also needs to read the router's state: what paths exist, what traffic is flowing, and whether a change it asked for actually took effect. The document notes that today's tools show only the paths that are active right now, not the ones that are switched off or unknown.

sections.title: What a Protocol for I2RS Would Have to Do
sections.content:
Section 5 lists the key aspects needed in an interface to the routing system. Whether such a protocol is built by extending existing mechanisms or requires a new mechanism requires further investigation.

Multiple simultaneous asynchronous operations. A single application should be able to send multiple independent atomic operations via I2RS without being required to wait for each to complete before sending the next. Very fine granularity of data locking for writing. When an I2RS operation is processed, the data locked for writing must be very granular, such as a particular prefix and route, rather than extremely coarse as it is for writing configuration; this improves the number of concurrent I2RS operations that are feasible and reduces blocking delays. Multi-headed control. Multiple applications may communicate to the same I2RS agent in a minimally coordinated fashion, and the agent must be able to handle multiple requests in a well-known policy-based fashion. Data written can be owned by different I2RS clients at different times, and may even be overwritten by a different I2RS client.

Duplex. Communications can be established by either the I2RS client, which resides within the application or is used by it to reach the agent, or by the I2RS agent. Events, acknowledgements, failures and operations can be sent at any time by both the router and the application, so I2RS is not a pure pull model where only the application queries to pull responses. High throughput. At a minimum, the I2RS agent and associated router should handle a considerable number of operations per second, for example 10,000 per second to handle many individual subscriber routes changing simultaneously. Low latency. Within a sub-second timescale it should be possible to complete simple operations such as reading or writing a single prefix route.

Multiple channels. Information should be communicable via the interface from different components in the router without going through a single channel. For example, for scaling, some exported data or events may be better sent directly from the forwarding plane, while other interactions come from the control plane. One channel, with authorisation and authentication, may be considered primary; only an authorised client can then request that information be delivered on a different channel. Writes from a client are only expected on channels that provide authorisation and authentication. Scalable, filterable information access. To extract information in a scalable fashion that is more easily used by applications, the ability to specify filtering constructs in an operation requesting data or requesting an asynchronous notification is very valuable. Secure control and access. Any ability to manipulate routing state must be subject to authentication and authorisation, sensitive routing information may need to be provided via secure access back to the client, such communications must be integrity protected, and most will also require confidentiality. Extensibility and interoperability. Both the protocol and the models must be extensible and interoperate between different versions of protocols and models.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of requirements is long but plain: many things at once, changes that lock as little as possible, several applications sharing one router, traffic in both directions, thousands of operations a second, answers in under a second, and everything authenticated and authorised.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security is a key aspect of any protocol that allows state installation and the extraction of detailed router state, and the need for secure control and access is one of the aspects listed in Section 5. More architectural security considerations are discussed in RFC 7921. In brief, the I2RS agent is assumed to have a separate authentication and authorisation channel by which it can validate both the identity and the permissions associated with an I2RS client. Mutual authentication between the agent and the client is required. Different levels of integrity, confidentiality and replay protection are relevant for different aspects of I2RS.
sections.plainLanguage: The short security section says the agent must have its own way of checking who a client is and what it is allowed to do, that both ends authenticate each other, and that different parts of the interface need different levels of protection against tampering, reading and replay.

viz.caption: The ten key aspects listed in Section 5

items.label: Multiple simultaneous asynchronous operations

items.desc: Several applications talk to the same agent in a minimally coordinated way.

items.label: Duplex
items.desc: Either end may open the connection and either end may send events or failures.

items.label: Low latency
items.desc: Simple operations complete on a sub-second timescale.

items.label: Multiple channels
items.desc: Data can come from different router components without a single channel.

items.label: Scalable, filterable information access
items.desc: Ask for only the data or notifications that are wanted.

items.label: Secure control and access
items.desc: Authentication, authorisation, integrity protection and confidentiality.

items.label: Extensibility and interoperability
items.desc: The protocol and models must work across different versions.
